title: Search Tree Keys Within Bounds
statement:
You get the root of a binary search tree with distinct keys: every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key, and every key in its right subtree is larger. You also get two numbers low ≤ high.

Return the sum of all keys k in the tree with low ≤ k ≤ high. Both bounds are inclusive. An empty tree, or a range that holds no key, gives 0.

examples.why: Keys 12, 20 and 25 fall inside the range: 12 + 20 + 25 = 57.
5 is too small, but its right child 7 is in range. Only the left side of a too-small node can be skipped.

hints: Visiting every node and adding the keys in range already works. What does the search-tree order let you skip?
If a node's key is below low, can anything in its left subtree be in range? What about its right subtree?
Recurse: key < low → only the right subtree; key > high → only the left subtree; otherwise add the key and visit both.

explain.intuition:
Any traversal that adds the in-range keys is correct. The search-tree order lets you prune. If a node's key is below low, its whole left subtree is even smaller, so only the right subtree can contribute. If the key is above high, only the left subtree can. Otherwise the node counts and both sides might too.

The common bug is pruning too much: a key below low does not mean its whole subtree is out, because its right side holds larger keys. The pruned walk visits roughly the in-range nodes plus one path along each boundary, instead of the whole tree.
steps: If the node is null, return 0.
If node.val < low, return the result for node.right.
If node.val > high, return the result for node.left.
Otherwise return node.val plus the results for both children.
pitfalls: Returning 0 as soon as a key is out of range, which drops in-range keys in the opposite subtree (the third example).
Using strict comparisons, so keys equal to low or high are left out.
Recursing on very deep, chain-shaped trees in a language with a small stack. An explicit stack avoids that.

complexity.time: O(n) worst case; O(h + k) for k keys in range when pruning

solutions.title: Visit every node
solutions.idea: Walk the whole tree with an explicit stack and add every key that falls in the range.

solutions.title: Pruned walk using the search-tree order
solutions.idea: Only descend into a subtree that can still contain keys in the range.

followups: You get many (low, high) questions on the same tree. How would you answer each in O(log n)? (Think subtree sums.)
Return the keys in range in sorted order instead of their sum.
